newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl confident about German economy for 1997.
newsitem.headline: Kohl confident about German economy for 1997.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl said he was confident economic growth in Germany would accelerate in 1997, and he expected to see improvement in unemployment this year.
Speaking to parliament, Kohl confirmed earlier forecasts that gross domestic product (GDP) will exand by 2.5 percent this year after 1.4 percent in 1996.
He said solid growth in world trade and a correction in the mark's exchange rate would add to growth this year.

"We expect economic growth to accelerate in 1997 to 2.5 percent from 1.4 percent in 1996," he said. "Our expectations have a solid foundation. World trade is expanding strongly, and the excessive revaluation of the mark from the spring of 1995 has receded."
Every fifth job in Germany depends on exports, he said.
The chancellor also affirmed that his government stands by its goal of halving unemployment by the decade's end.

"We expect to have a turnaround on the job market this year," he said. The number of unemployed will average 4.1 million this year, he said, adding that unemployment will decline in the second half after peaking in the spring.

"We will halve unemployment by the end of the decade," Kohl said. "It is an ambitious goal, and no one can do all that alone. Everyone has to work together towards that goal -- unions, employers and government."
He said the jobless rate could drop and between 100,000 and 200,000 new jobs be created if companies cut overtime hours and urged creation of more part-time jobs.
The 1.8 billion hours in overtime worked each year was simply too much, Kohl said.
"We are talking about the solidarity of those with jobs and those without jobs," Kohl said.
He predicted two million part-time jobs could be created.
Discussing the high unemployment rate, Kohl said women had filled two million of the three million new jobs created in western Germany in the last decade.

Kohl said the percentage of women working in western Germany had climbed from 46 percent in 1970 to 60 percent currently. The increase in the number of women in the workforce had made a clear impact on the job market, he said.
"The consequences cannot be overlooked," Kohl said.
Kohl said a contributing factor to high unemployment was the 1.1 million foreign immigrants in Germany in 1995, even more than the 720,000 who immigrated to the United States in that year.
